title: Production GenAI Systems
topic: production generative AI systems: taking LLM and agent applications from pilot to production
subtitle: Seventeen practitioners — Databricks, AWS, MongoDB, Red Hat, Factory, Caylent, Azure AI Search, IBM, Resolve AI, and two agencies that ship client work every fortnight — on the distance between a pilot that impressed the room and a system that survives Monday morning. Everything below is traceable to a chunk you can open.

sources.title: Production-Grade AI Project Tutorial – Build & Deploy
sources.contributed: A hands-on build of an 'enterprise-grade' Python training-data curation system, showing concrete software-architecture patterns for productionizing a GenAI data pipeline: unified/abstract loaders, Pydantic data models, async context managers, task-template driven generation, a multi-provider AI client with simulation fallback, a quality evaluator, and a multi-format exporter.

sources.title: From GenAI Pilots to Production - Nikita Kozodoi
sources.contributed: Field-tested, project-grounded advice from AWS's GenAI Innovation Center: layered/independent guardrail architecture, red-teaming practice, human-then-LLM-judge evaluation pipelines, concrete fine-tuning cost and data-volume thresholds, and organizational discipline (scoping, 'simplest tool first') for getting pilots into production.

sources.title: How I Build and Ship Custom AI Solutions for Clients
sources.contributed: The only talk with the business/process layer around production GenAI: discovery-call red flags, accuracy-expectation management (70/80% to 90%), PoC vs MVP framing, sprint pricing, and the standardized deploy/monitor/secure stack (Hetzner, Caddy, Langfuse, Sentry).

sources.title: GenAI in Production: How RAG & AI Agents Are Shaping the Future
sources.contributed: Interview-format breakdown of the RAG stack, agent vs. chatbot distinctions, a concrete case study (60% retrieval-time reduction), and a checklist of production hurdles (security, monitoring, rollout patterns, risks) from an applied-AI engineering consultant.

sources.title: The Production AI Playbook: Deploying Agents at Enterprise Scale — Sandipan Bhaumik, Databricks
sources.contributed: An end-to-end enterprise playbook (five pillars: evaluation, observability, data foundation, orchestration, governance) grounded in a real banking-chatbot case study with dollar and time figures.

sources.title: Always-on agents run production without the on-call tax — Justin Smith, Resolve AI
sources.contributed: The 'background agent' pattern for production operations: always-on, cloud-sandboxed agents triggered by schedule/event/message that absorb the uncounted long tail of on-call work (deployment monitoring, health checks, handoffs, Slack triage), with the agent itself deciding how long and how often to keep checking.

sources.title: POC to PROD: Hard Lessons from 200+ Enterprise GenAI Deployments - Randall Hunt, Caylent
sources.contributed: Tactical, war-story lessons from 200+ enterprise deployments: concrete cost/speed tradeoffs across AWS vector stores and custom silicon, prompt-caching mechanics, generative UI, and 'know your user' field failures (low-connectivity PDFs, nurses rejecting voice bots).

sources.title: Build a Complete End-to-End GenAI Project in 3 Hours
sources.contributed: A real-time, warts-and-all build of an AI news aggregator from brainstorm to Render deployment — shows the actual AI-assisted planning workflow, the specific production failures hit (OOM from a heavy library, duplicate digests, exposed database, env-mixups) and how each was fixed.

sources.title: AI Infrastructure Explained (GPUs, vLLM, and LLM-D)
sources.contributed: The only talk in the cluster that goes underneath the application layer: GPU vs CPU architecture, VRAM bandwidth math, tokens/prefill/decode/KV-cache mechanics, batching limits, sharding strategies, and the LLM-D router/well-lit-path recipes for running vLLM fleets on Kubernetes.

sources.title: Scalable GenAI in Production - Kamelia Aryafar
sources.contributed: Practitioner lessons from scaling GenAI at Netflix/Google-scale: the full production stack, a 5-stage maturity model, the 'latency is a product decision' framing, the data-flywheel/continuous-evaluation argument, and five imperatives for taking GenAI from demo to system.

sources.title: Exploring MLOps and LLMOps: Architectures and Best Practices
sources.contributed: Databricks' platform-level view: the deploy-code-not-deploy-models pattern, Unity Catalog governance/lineage, Lakehouse Monitoring driving automated drift-triggered retraining, and a framework for what specifically changes in LLMOps (model selection, data, evaluation, deploy/monitor) versus classic MLOps, plus MLflow tracing/packaging specifics for chains.

sources.title: Make GenAI Production-Ready With Kubernetes Patterns - Roland Huss, Red Hat & Bilgin Ibryam, Diagrid
sources.contributed: Maps established Kubernetes patterns onto GenAI workloads: model-data loading tricks (init container, model-car sidecar hack, image volumes), LLM-state-aware request routing (prefix/KV-cache-aware, prefill/decode disaggregation), and RAG as a composed pattern of existing primitives.

sources.title: AI System Design: From Idea to Production - Apoorva Joshi, MongoDB
sources.contributed: A repeatable four-phase framework (product requirements -> system design -> evaluation/monitoring -> cost/latency/reliability optimization) walked step-by-step through a hypothetical health-insurance claims review system, including how to pick retrieval patterns and set concrete guardrail metrics.

sources.title: RAG at scale: production ready GenAI apps with Azure AI Search
sources.contributed: Retrieval-layer scaling mechanics for RAG in production — two-stage recall+rerank, quantization tradeoffs, index density limits, and ingestion pipelines — from the team building Azure AI Search.

sources.title: The Multi-Agent Architecture That Actually Ships — Luke Alvoeiro, Factory
sources.contributed: A concrete production multi-agent architecture (Factory's 'missions') for long-horizon coding work: orchestrator/worker/validator roles, adversarial validation contracts, serial-not-parallel execution, and per-role model selection.

sources.title: Omnigent: Open-Source Meta-Harness for AI Agents | Matei Zaharia
sources.contributed: The only talk on infrastructure for running many coding agents together: session portability across models, contextual (state-aware) security policies, per-agent spend caps, and the case for open-sourcing the orchestration layer.

sources.title: Large Language Model Operations (LLMOps) Explained
sources.contributed: Short vendor-agnostic primer that names the LLMOps lifecycle stages and explains how LLM-specific requirements (transfer learning, cost-aware tuning, BLEU/ROUGE evaluation) diverge from traditional MLOps.

gaps: None of the three talks give concrete guidance on who owns or is on-call for the AI agent itself once it's in production (who debugs the debugger).
No talk details how to red-team, adversarially test, or defend against prompt injection for a production agent with real autonomy.
The claims-review system in T0HhO4YtTfE is a hypothetical walkthrough, not a shipped case study -- there are no real production latency, cost, or accuracy numbers for it once live.
vSx5IULvBns doesn't explain how Resolve evaluates or scores whether a background agent's own actions/investigations were actually correct -- no eval methodology for the agent's judgment is given.
vW8wLsb3Nnc doesn't describe how prompts or evals are version-controlled, reviewed, or rolled back in CI for the 200+ deployments referenced.
None of the talks name specific multi-agent orchestration frameworks (e.g. LangGraph, CrewAI) -- 'orchestration frameworks' is mentioned only generically in T0HhO4YtTfE.
No talk addresses how to handle model deprecation or migration risk at scale beyond the single anecdote of Claude 3.7 to 4 being a drop-in upgrade.

None of the three talks give concrete dollar or token-cost figures for running retrieval/rerank infrastructure or multi-agent missions at steady-state production volume (Factory mentions prompt caching helps, but not by how much; Azure talk gives no pricing).

The Databricks talk shows a vector database going stale (policy doc embeddings not refreshed) as a real incident, but none of the three videos describe a concrete freshness/refresh strategy (e.g., cadence, staleness alarms) to prevent this proactively rather than detect it after CSAT drops.
No talk addresses how to choose which specific cross-encoder or reranker model to deploy beyond citing Azure's ~100ms budget — no comparative guidance on reranker model selection.
Factory's talk does not explain how the hundreds of assertions in a validation contract are authored, reviewed, or kept from becoming stale as requirements change over a 16-30 day mission.
None of the talks detail concrete prompt-injection or adversarial-input defenses for agents that call external tools/APIs in production, beyond generic mentions of guardrail checks and PII detection.

The Azure AI Search talk does not address multi-agent orchestration at all, and the two agent-orchestration talks (Factory, Databricks) do not address vector index scaling/quantization — a reader wanting both retrieval-infra scaling and agent-orchestration scaling has to synthesize across talks with no single source of truth on how they interact (e.g., how RAG retrieval scaling interacts with multi-agent tool calls).
None of the three talks give concrete production inference cost figures (e.g. $ per million tokens or $/GPU-hour at serving scale) — only fine-tuning hourly costs are quantified.
No comparison of specific vector database products or benchmarks for RAG retrieval quality/latency at production scale.
The Kubernetes talk describes prefix/KV-cache-aware routing conceptually but does not detail the protocol or latency cost of the cache-eviction signaling between LLM servers and the endpoint picker.
No guidance on GPU cluster autoscaling thresholds or capacity-planning numbers for handling production traffic spikes.
No discussion of multi-region failover or disaster-recovery strategy specific to GenAI serving.
No data on false-positive/false-negative rates for the guardrail classifier fleets described by Nikita — only latency and layering, not accuracy tradeoffs.
No guidance on team sizing, budget, or ROI-measurement benchmarks for standing up a scoping/'AI strategist' function.

The evaluation walkthroughs (score sheets, LLM-as-judge) are demonstrated mainly on a translation use case; no detail on how the same rubric-based approach generalizes to open-ended agentic or multi-turn chat evaluation.

None of the three talks give a worked methodology for LLM evaluation scoring (e.g. how accuracy percentages like the '70-80% to 90%' figures were actually measured) beyond mentioning that evals exist.
No discussion of fine-tuning versus prompting/RAG as a lever for improving accuracy on a stuck use case.
No detail on how Omnigen's 'intelligent routing' heuristics are trained or how reliable that routing actually is.
No discussion of latency or SLA requirements for production agent responses, or how those trade off against cost/accuracy.

The client-facing playbook (Q679gH7oszg) is agency/freelancer-specific (proposals, sprint billing); none of the talks address how the same discovery-to-production process maps onto an internal enterprise platform team without external client billing.
No breakdown of ongoing per-token / per-request LLM API costs at production volume, despite spend-cap tooling being discussed (only a $1,000 mistaken-spend anecdote is given).
No discussion of how to roll out or roll back changes to prompts/agents already in production (canary releases, A/B testing, versioning of prompts).

No concrete $/token or $/GPU-hour cost figures for a real production deployment — the Netflix talk names cost as a top imperative but gives no numbers, and the infra talk covers hardware specs without pricing.
No detail on how to technically implement input/output guardrails or policy enforcement (e.g. which libraries, filters, or classifiers) beyond naming the four responsible-AI buckets.
No discussion of security testing, red-teaming, or prompt-injection defenses for agentic systems.
No walkthrough of how to actually build an LLM-judge pipeline (prompt design, calibration against humans, golden dataset construction) — it's named as important but not shown.
No comparison of vLLM against other inference engines (TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, TGI) or guidance on when to choose one over another.
No numbers or case study on what organizational alignment work actually looks like in practice, despite it being named as one of the five imperatives.
No discussion of how to size or validate a fine-tuning dataset, or what fine-tuning costs/timelines look like in practice.
No treatment of multi-region or disaster-recovery concerns for GPU fleets serving global traffic.
Neither video gives concrete infrastructure cost numbers (e.g. $/query, $/1M tokens, GPU hosting cost) beyond generic warnings that 'costs can spiral' — a reader can't budget from this corpus alone.

mvleESOUTRw's quality evaluator (toxicity, bias, diversity, coherence, relevance checks) is explicitly left as a 'mock' / unimplemented stub, so there's no concrete method or threshold for scoring generated data, only the category names.

Neither talk names a specific evaluation framework or benchmark (e.g. RAGAS, human-eval rubrics with numeric thresholds) for judging RAG answer quality — uaiq1HvQKoI says evaluation is 'notoriously difficult' but doesn't prescribe a method.
No discussion in either video of specific multi-agent orchestration frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen) by name, despite both discussing agents/task managers conceptually.
Neither video reports concrete latency/throughput numbers or load-test results for a production RAG or agent system.

mvleESOUTRw leaves classification and summarization task generators, additional export formats, and toxicity/bias detection unimplemented ('please feel free to go ahead and implement that'), so the guide can't cite a working reference implementation for those pieces from this corpus.
Neither video addresses fine-tuning workflows in production detail (only a passing warning that fine-tuned models inherit bad training data).
